title: Gimel runs to dalet (Shabbat 104a)
hook: the rabbis say gimel's foot runs after dalet: the giver chases the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, bet: closed on three sides, open toward what comes next. Your line was bet is a house. Did you pause at your door? Today, the third and fourth letters, and what they do together. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

The Talmud tells a story about a classroom turned upside down. Some young children walk into the house of study, where the rabbis sit with their books, and the children start teaching. Not reciting. Teaching. They go through the alphabet letter by letter and explain what each one is saying. And the rabbis write it down. The Talmud is impressed enough to say that nothing like it had been heard in a very long time. When the children reach the third and fourth letters, gimel and dalet, they point at something tiny in the way the letters are drawn. A foot. Today's word is where that foot is going.
screen: `CHILDREN IN THE HOUSE OF STUDY.` → `THEY TEACH THE RABBIS.` → `GIMEL, DALET, AND A FOOT.`

segments.voice: Gimel runs to dalet. Turn it four ways. First, the two letters as a phrase. The children read gimel dalet as gemol dalim: be kind to the poor. Gimel stands for the giver. Dalet stands for the one in need. Second, the foot. Gimel is drawn with a little leg reaching out at the bottom, toward the left, toward dalet, which comes next. Why? Because, the children say, it is the way of someone who does kindness to run after the poor. Not to sit at home and wait for a knock. To go looking. Third, dalet's answer. Dalet has a leg of its own, reaching back toward gimel. That, they say, is so the poor person makes themselves available to be found. But dalet's face is turned away from gimel. Why? So the gift is given in secret, and the one receiving it is not ashamed. Two letters, and between them a whole way of giving: run toward the need, and then look away while it's met. Fourth, the giving itself. Giving only when asked, or only when seen, asks little. These two letters ask something harder. Notice the need before anyone has to say it. Close the distance yourself. And protect the other person's dignity while you do it, so that what they remember is the help, not the embarrassment. The children in the study house found all of that in a foot and a turned face. Tomorrow we stay with dalet.
screen: `GEMOL DALIM: BE KIND TO THE POOR.` · `GIMEL'S FOOT RUNS TOWARD DALET.` · `DALET'S FACE TURNS AWAY.` · `NOTICE, RUN, PROTECT.` · then, large: `GIMEL RUNS TO DALET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: run toward one need. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a need near you that nobody has asked you to meet. A neighbor stretched thin. A coworker short this month. A food bank down the road. Hold it for a while. Then choose one gift you could give today, and one way to give it so that the person doesn't have to feel watched: a quiet transfer, groceries left at the door, a donation with no name on it. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Gimel runs to dalet. The Talmud's reading of two letters: gemol dalim, the giver running after the poor, and giving quietly. Today's word.
Your line: gimel runs to dalet. Today, give the gift you chose, before anyone asks, and keep it quiet. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on tzedakah, giving to those in need, prizes giving that seeks out the need and spares the receiver shame; the Talmud reads this into the shapes of gimel and dalet.

original.note: Hebrew: be kind to the poor, the Talmud's reading of gimel and dalet.

trapdoor: what you thought: gimel and dalet are just the third and fourth letters.
what it means: the Talmud reads them as gemol dalim, be kind to the poor, with gimel's foot running after dalet.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 104a — dalet's leg reaches back so the poor can be found, and its face turns away so the gift is given in secret.

notes: Editor pass: replaced the stock 'an ordinary Tuesday' turn (also used in day 1322's draft) with 'the giving itself', and reworded its first line.

Shabbat 104a paraphrased throughout: children in the study house; gimel dalet as gemol dalim; gimel's leg stretched toward dalet (the way of the benevolent to run after the poor); dalet's leg toward gimel (so the poor make themselves available); dalet's face turned away (give in secret so he is not ashamed). Confirm the retelling.
The Talmud's remark that such things were not said even in the days of Joshua bin Nun is softened to 'nothing like it had been heard in a very long time'; confirm, or restore the reference.
Dalet's own meanings (delet, door; dal, poor) are left mostly for tomorrow (day 1332).
